classification.difficultyReason: Use polynomial long division to establish a zero remainder, then factorise the quotient and divisor completely.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use long division to prove that $P(x)=x^3+x^2-41x-105$ is divisible by $x+5$. Hence, factorise $P(x)$ completely.

answer.short:
$P(x)=(x+5)(x+3)(x-7)$.

Long division gives quotient $x^2-4x-21$ and remainder $0$.
answer.worked:
The successive quotient terms are $x^2$, $-4x$ and $-21$.
$$\begin{array}{r}x^2-4x-21\\\hline x+5\,\big)\,x^3+x^2-41x-105\end{array}$$
$$\begin{align*}(x^3+x^2-41x-105)-(x^3+5x^2)&=-4x^2-41x-105\\(-4x^2-41x-105)-(-4x^2-20x)&=-21x-105\\(-21x-105)-(-21x-105)&=0\end{align*}$$
The remainder is zero, so $P(x)$ is divisible by $x+5$.
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=(x+5)(x^2-4x-21)\\P(x)&=(x+5)(x+3)(x-7).\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use long division to prove that $P(x)=x^4+10x^3+37x^2+60x+36$ is divisible by $x^2+4x+4$. Hence, factorise $P(x)$ completely.

answer.short:
$P(x)=(x+2)^2(x+3)^2$.

Long division gives quotient $x^2+6x+9$ and remainder $0$.
answer.worked:
The successive quotient terms are $x^2$, $6x$ and $9$.
$$\begin{array}{r}x^2+6x+9\\\hline x^2+4x+4\,\big)\,x^4+10x^3+37x^2+60x+36\end{array}$$
$$\begin{align*}(x^4+10x^3+37x^2+60x+36)-(x^4+4x^3+4x^2)&=6x^3+33x^2+60x+36\\(6x^3+33x^2+60x+36)-(6x^3+24x^2+24x)&=9x^2+36x+36\\(9x^2+36x+36)-(9x^2+36x+36)&=0\end{align*}$$
The remainder is zero, so $P(x)$ is divisible by $x^2+4x+4$.
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=(x^2+4x+4)(x^2+6x+9)\\P(x)&=(x+2)^2(x+3)^2.\end{align*}$$
